entries.meaning: The modal of ability, permission, and possibility: can in the present, could for the past and for polite or hypothetical use — and no participle at all, so the perfect is have been able to.
examples: I can carry both bags if you get the door.
She could swim before she turned four.
We could not find a parking spot anywhere downtown.
I can read Spanish well enough, but I can't speak it.
He can play three instruments.
By the end of the summer she could ride without training wheels.
You can park on this side after six.
Back then you could still buy a ticket at the gate.
Students cannot register until their fees are paid.
Can you hold the door for a second?
Could you say that again a little slower?
Can I get you anything from the kitchen?
Winters here can get brutal.
That intersection can be dangerous in the rain.
The old road could wash out after a heavy rain.
That can't be right — check the total again.
He couldn't have known; nobody told him.
She can't be more than twenty.
We could leave now if you want to beat the traffic.
You could have called instead of driving all the way over.
Could we move the meeting to Thursday?
I can see the ocean from the top floor.
We could hear them arguing through the wall.
Can you smell that?
I can't help laughing every time he tells that story.
She couldn't help noticing the missing signature.
He can't help it — he was raised that way.
Since the surgery he has been able to walk without a cane — never ✗ has could.
By March we had been able to clear most of the backlog.
She could not get through on the phone, and she has not been able to since.

senses.head: Be able to (ability)
body: The core sense: the subject has the strength, the power, or the opportunity to do something. Could covers past ability and also softens a present claim. (мочь, быть в состоянии)
examples: I can carry both bags if you get the door.
She could swim before she turned four.
We could not find a parking spot anywhere downtown.

senses.head: Know how to (learned skill)
body: Where Russian uses уметь: a skill acquired by learning rather than a one-time possibility. English does not mark the difference — can does both jobs. (уметь)
examples: I can read Spanish well enough, but I can't speak it.
He can play three instruments.
By the end of the summer she could ride without training wheels.

senses.head: Be allowed to (permission)
body: Permission granted by a rule or by a person. May is the formal equivalent, but American speech uses can almost everywhere. (можно, иметь право)
examples: You can park on this side after six.
Back then you could still buy a ticket at the gate.
Students cannot register until their fees are paid.

senses.head: Requests and offers — Can you…?
body: Can you asks someone to do something; Can I offers or asks permission. Could here is politeness, not past time — the most useful thing to know in the whole entry. (не могли бы вы; можно мне)
examples: Can you hold the door for a second?
Could you say that again a little slower?
Can I get you anything from the kitchen?

senses.head: Possibility — what sometimes happens
body: A general or occasional possibility, not a prediction about one occasion; for a specific guess about the future English uses may or might. (бывает, может случиться)
examples: Winters here can get brutal.
That intersection can be dangerous in the rain.
The old road could wash out after a heavy rain.

senses.head: can't — impossibility, confident deduction
body: Negative can't is the strong "that is impossible" counterpart of must: not a lack of ability but a refusal to believe. In past time it is can't have or couldn't have. (не может быть, никак не может)
examples: That can't be right — check the total again.
He couldn't have known; nobody told him.
She can't be more than twenty.

senses.head: could — hypothetical, suggestion, missed chance
body: A present or future hypothetical, a soft suggestion, or — with have — something that was possible and did not happen. The time reference is not past, despite the form. (мог бы; можно было бы)
examples: We could leave now if you want to beat the traffic.
You could have called instead of driving all the way over.
Could we move the meeting to Thursday?

senses.head: can see, can hear — perception
body: With verbs of perception and mental state, can carries the load a progressive would carry elsewhere: ✗ I am hearing you comes out as I can hear you. (вижу, слышу (сейчас))
examples: I can see the ocean from the top floor.
We could hear them arguing through the wall.
Can you smell that?

senses.head: can't help — be unable to stop yourself
body: A fixed frame, always negative, followed by an -ing form or by it: ✗ can't help to laugh. (не могу удержаться, ничего не могу поделать)
examples: I can't help laughing every time he tells that story.
She couldn't help noticing the missing signature.
He can't help it — he was raised that way.

senses.head: No participle — use be able to
body: Could is a past tense, not a real participle: English has no ✗ I have could and no ✗ to can. Wherever a perfect, an infinitive, or a future is needed, be able to takes over. (смочь (в перфекте и инфинитиве))
examples: Since the surgery he has been able to walk without a cane — never ✗ has could.
By March we had been able to clear most of the backlog.
She could not get through on the phone, and she has not been able to since.

entries.pronunciation note: weak form /kən/ in I can go
entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.pattern: an — ould (a modal, not an ordinary verb)
entries.third person: can — no -s, ✗ he cans · -ing form: none; modals have no -ing and no infinitive
entries.contrast: Could is a past tense, not a real participle: English has no ✗ I have could. Where a perfect is needed, be able to takes over — I have been able to drive since I was seventeen. Could also serves as a present-tense politeness or a hypothetical (Could you hold this?, We could leave now), so a could in front of you is not automatically about the past. The l is silent, as in would and should. A separate and fully regular can means "put food in cans": canned, canning.
entries.verb type: modal auxiliary — never a main verb: it takes a bare infinitive (can carry), has no -s, no -ing, and no participle (✗ he cans, ✗ I have could, ✗ to can), so be able to fills the perfect and infinitive slots. A separate, fully regular action verb can means "put food in cans."
entries.transitivity: neither transitive nor intransitive in the ordinary sense — a modal takes a bare-infinitive complement, not an object: I can carry both bags. The only nominal object it ever shows is the fixed he can't help it.
entries.passive: no — modals have no passive of their own; voice is carried by the verb they support (the bags can be carried), never by can itself.

entries.meaning: Put clothing on someone or supply them with it — and, as clad, cover a surface as if with clothing.
examples: The shelter clothes and feeds about forty families every winter.
They had almost nothing to clothe the children in.
By noon the volunteers had clothed and fed two hundred people.
The reactor core is clad in steel.
Every wall of the lobby had been clad in walnut.
They clad the new tower in blue glass.
Snow clad the hills overnight.
Fog clothes the valley most mornings.
By dawn the fields had been clad in frost.
Two scantily clad dancers came out for the finale.
The hikers arrived clad in bright rain gear.

senses.head: Dress someone, supply clothing
body: Transitive, and usually paired with feed. In this everyday sense the regular clothed is the normal American past and participle; clad would sound biblical. (одевать, обеспечивать одеждой)
examples: The shelter clothes and feeds about forty families every winter.
They had almost nothing to clothe the children in.
By noon the volunteers had clothed and fed two hundred people.

senses.head: be clad in — faced, sheathed
body: Technical and architectural, nearly always passive and followed by in: a surface covered with a protective or decorative material. (быть облицованным, покрытым (чем-л.))
examples: The reactor core is clad in steel.
Every wall of the lobby had been clad in walnut.
They clad the new tower in blue glass.

senses.head: Cover as if with clothing
body: Literary, of snow, fog, ivy, or light lying over a landscape. Clad is the usual form here. (окутывать, покрывать)
examples: Snow clad the hills overnight.
Fog clothes the valley most mornings.
By dawn the fields had been clad in frost.

senses.head: clad as an adjective
body: The participle does most of its modern work as an adjective, either with a modifier in front (scantily clad, poorly clad) or inside a compound (ivy-clad, steel-clad). (одетый (во что-л.))
examples: Two scantily clad dancers came out for the finale.
The hikers arrived clad in bright rain gear.

entries.pronunciation note: the th of the, not of thin
entries.register: neutral to formal — ordinary in writing (clothe and feed), uncommon in speech, where an American says dress or put clothes on
entries.third person: clothes /kloʊðz/ · -ing form: clothing (spelled like the noun clothing)
entries.contrast: In ordinary American English the past and participle are the regular clothed — the shelter clothed and fed them. Clad is the older form, and it survives mostly as a participial adjective, almost always with in or inside a compound: scantily clad, ivy-clad, steel-clad. Both are standard; clad is literary or technical, clothed is what goes in a report. Keep the verb clothe /kloʊð/ apart from the noun cloth /klɔθ/, whose th is voiceless and whose plural is cloths.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, from supplying clothing (the shelter clothes and feeds them) to covering a surface (snow clad the hills). The participle clad now does most of its work as an adjective: scantily clad, ivy-clad.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is obligatory: clothe the children, ✗ the shelter clothed on its own. The facing sense adds in: they clad the new tower in blue glass.
entries.passive: yes, and the be clad in sense is normally passive — the reactor core is clad in steel, every wall of the lobby had been clad in walnut.

entries.meaning: Run from danger — leave a place or a person quickly in order to escape.
examples: Families flee the coast whenever a hurricane is forecast.
Thousands fled the city in a single week.
She has fled two wars and hopes never to do it again.
The driver had fled the scene before officers arrived.
He fled the country a week ahead of the indictment.
Two of the suspects have fled the state.
He flees any conversation that turns to money.
Young doctors are fleeing rural practice.
Sleep fled the moment the phone rang.
All the color had fled her face.

senses.head: Escape from danger
body: The core sense. The object comes bare in edited American prose — fled the city — though flee from also occurs. Do not confuse fled with flew, which belongs to fly. (бежать, спасаться бегством)
examples: Families flee the coast whenever a hurricane is forecast.
Thousands fled the city in a single week.
She has fled two wars and hopes never to do it again.

senses.head: Flee justice, abscond
body: Legal and journalistic: leaving to avoid arrest, prosecution, or a court order. Common in flee the scene and flee the country. (скрываться, бежать (от правосудия))
examples: The driver had fled the scene before officers arrived.
He fled the country a week ahead of the indictment.
Two of the suspects have fled the state.

senses.head: Avoid, keep away from
body: Figurative and somewhat formal: shunning a subject, a duty, or a kind of company rather than a physical danger. (избегать, бежать от)
examples: He flees any conversation that turns to money.
Young doctors are fleeing rural practice.

senses.head: Vanish, slip away (of abstract things)
body: Literary. Sleep, color, hope, and daylight flee rather than simply going away. (исчезать, улетучиваться)
examples: Sleep fled the moment the phone rang.
All the color had fled her face.

entries.register: neutral — standard in news and narrative (fled the scene); conversation usually says run or get out
entries.third person: flees · -ing form: fleeing (the e stays — ✗ fleing)
entries.contrast: Fled and flew belong to different verbs. Flee/fled/fled is escaping; fly/flew/flown is air travel: the family fled the country, but the family flew to Denver. Flee takes its object bare — fled the city — where learners often write fled from the city; both occur, but the bare object is the one in edited American prose.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout, including the literary use with abstract subjects: sleep fled the moment the phone rang, all the color had fled her face.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with a bare object in edited American prose (fled the city, fled the scene, fled the country), intransitive or with from when the danger is left unnamed (families flee whenever a hurricane is forecast).
entries.passive: restricted — grammatical but avoided: ✗ the scene was fled by the driver reads badly, and writers keep the active. The intransitive use has no passive at all.

entries.meaning: Say in advance that something will happen — the vocabulary of prophecy rather than of forecasting.
examples: The old almanac claimed to foretell the winter from the thickness of the corn husks.
Two economists foretold the collapse and were ignored.
He foretold his own retirement a year before he announced it.
Nothing in the data foretells a crash.
The opening chapter had foretold the ending, and nobody noticed.
Everything that letter has foretold has come true.

senses.head: Prophesy, predict
body: Of a person or a text announcing the future. Formal and literary; for ordinary predictions American English uses predict for events and forecast for weather and numbers. (предсказывать, пророчить)
examples: The old almanac claimed to foretell the winter from the thickness of the corn husks.
Two economists foretold the collapse and were ignored.
He foretold his own retirement a year before he announced it.

senses.head: Be a sign of what is coming
body: With an inanimate subject — data, an omen, an opening chapter — meaning that it points to a later outcome. No intention is involved. (предвещать, предзнаменовать)
examples: Nothing in the data foretells a crash.
The opening chapter had foretold the ending, and nobody noticed.
Everything that letter has foretold has come true.

entries.register: rare — recognized but seldom produced; prophecy and literature, while an American predicts an election and forecasts the weather
entries.third person: foretells · -ing form: foretelling (nothing doubles — tell already ends in a double l)
entries.contrast: It inflects exactly like tell; only the meaning is special. Foretell belongs to prophecy and literature — in everyday American writing you predict an election and forecast the weather, and you save foretold for oracles, omens, and anything that reads as fate.
entries.verb type: action with a human subject prophesying (two economists foretold the collapse); closer to stative with an inanimate subject that merely points to an outcome — nothing in the data foretells a crash, ✗ the data is foretelling a crash.
entries.transitivity: transitive — object obligatory, either a noun or a that-clause: foretold his own retirement, foretold that the deal would fail. ✗ He foretold alone is incomplete.
entries.passive: yes — the collapse was foretold and nobody listened; the ending had been foretold in the opening chapter.

entries.meaning: Take in a sound — and by extension get news, get word from someone, or listen formally to a case.
examples: I hear the train from my bedroom every night.
Do you hear that clicking noise?
Nobody heard the alarm go off.
She heard the news from a neighbor.
I hear you're moving to Denver.
We had heard about the layoffs before the memo went out.
We have heard nothing from the landlord since April.
Did you ever hear from your sister?
He heard from the school on Tuesday.
I have never heard of that band.
Nobody had heard of him before the trial.
Have you heard of a town called Winslow?
The judge hears motions on Thursday mornings.
The committee heard testimony for six hours.
The board has heard three appeals this month.
Hear me out before you say no.
They never heard her out.
Once he had heard them out, he changed his position.
I offered to pay and she wouldn't hear of it.
My father would not hear of my dropping out.
I hear you, but the budget won't stretch that far.
She said she heard me, and then did exactly what she wanted.

senses.head: Perceive a sound
body: Involuntary perception, not the deliberate act of listen: hearing happens to you. It resists the progressive — say I can hear you, not ✗ I am hearing you. (слышать)
examples: I hear the train from my bedroom every night.
Do you hear that clicking noise?
Nobody heard the alarm go off.

senses.head: Learn, get news of
body: Followed by a that-clause or by about. The simple present often reports something quite recent: I hear you're moving. (слышать, узнавать (новость))
examples: She heard the news from a neighbor.
I hear you're moving to Denver.
We had heard about the layoffs before the memo went out.

senses.head: hear from — get word from someone
body: Contact from a person, in any medium. Extremely common in the negative perfect: haven't heard from him. (получать известия от кого-л.)
examples: We have heard nothing from the landlord since April.
Did you ever hear from your sister?
He heard from the school on Tuesday.

senses.head: hear of — know that something exists
body: Almost always negative or interrogative: never heard of it. Distinct from hear about, which is about news rather than bare existence. (слышать о ком-л./чём-л.)
examples: I have never heard of that band.
Nobody had heard of him before the trial.
Have you heard of a town called Winslow?

senses.head: Hear a case, take testimony
body: Legal and institutional: a judge, a board, or a committee formally receives argument or evidence. (заслушивать, рассматривать (дело))
examples: The judge hears motions on Thursday mornings.
The committee heard testimony for six hours.
The board has heard three appeals this month.

senses.head: hear someone out — listen to the end
body: Separable, and usually imperative or negative; it implies the listener was ready to interrupt. (выслушать до конца)
examples: Hear me out before you say no.
They never heard her out.
Once he had heard them out, he changed his position.

senses.head: won't hear of it — refuse to allow
body: A fixed negative frame with will or would, rejecting a suggestion outright — often a generous one. (и слышать не хотеть)
examples: I offered to pay and she wouldn't hear of it.
My father would not hear of my dropping out.

senses.head: I hear you — I take your point
body: A conversational American formula acknowledging what someone said, usually right before disagreeing or naming a limit. Informal. (понимаю тебя; слышу тебя)
examples: I hear you, but the budget won't stretch that far.
She said she heard me, and then did exactly what she wanted.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.third person: hears · -ing form: hearing (also the noun — a hearing)
entries.contrast: The spelling adds one letter, but the vowel changes completely: hear rhymes with near, heard rhymes with bird — /hɝd/, never ✗ /hɪrd/. Spoken aloud, heard and herd are identical. And hear is not listen: hearing happens to you, listening is something you do (I heard the alarm / I listened to the message), which is why hear resists the progressive — say I can hear you, not ✗ I am hearing you.
entries.verb type: stative in the core perception sense, which rejects the progressive: ✗ I am hearing you — say I can hear you. Action in the deliberate institutional senses hear a case, hear the testimony, hear someone out.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object may be a noun, a that-clause, or a small clause (nobody heard the alarm go off). It is intransitive only with a preposition attached: hear from the landlord, hear of that band, wouldn't hear of it.
entries.passive: yes — the alarm was heard three blocks away, the committee heard testimony → testimony was heard for six hours, the senator was heard to say it. Even the prepositional sense passivizes in the fixed he has not been heard from since April.
entries.phrasal verbs: hear about · hear about, hear from, hear of · hear from · hear of · hear out

entries.meaning: Hear something and get it wrong — take one word for another.
examples: In a crowded room it is easy to mishear a name.
I misheard the gate number and nearly missed the flight.
She had misheard "fifteen" as "fifty."
He regularly mishears song lyrics and sings them wrong for years.
I must have misheard — did you say Tuesday or Thursday?
If I have misheard you, please say it again.

senses.head: Hear something incorrectly
body: You did hear it; you simply got it wrong. Failing to hear at all is didn't hear or couldn't hear, never mishear. Often built with as. (ослышаться, неправильно расслышать)
examples: In a crowded room it is easy to mishear a name.
I misheard the gate number and nearly missed the flight.
She had misheard "fifteen" as "fifty."
He regularly mishears song lyrics and sings them wrong for years.

senses.head: must have misheard — take the blame for a mix-up
body: The verb's most common home is this polite perfect formula, where the speaker takes responsibility for a misunderstanding rather than accusing the other person of misspeaking. (должно быть, я ослышался)
examples: I must have misheard — did you say Tuesday or Thursday?
If I have misheard you, please say it again.

entries.register: neutral — a prefixed derivative, but a live one: sorry, I must have misheard you is ordinary speech
entries.third person: mishears · -ing form: mishearing (also a noun: a common mishearing of the lyric)
entries.contrast: Inflects like hear. It means you heard something and got it wrong — not that you failed to hear it; for that, American English says didn't hear or couldn't hear. The verb is most at home in the perfect after must: I must have misheard.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and momentary, a single mishap rather than the ongoing state of hear: I misheard the gate number.
entries.transitivity: transitive, often with an as-complement (she had misheard "fifteen" as "fifty"). The object drops when it is recoverable — I must have misheard is complete.
entries.passive: restricted — natural in the as frame (the name is regularly misheard as Cohen), but the verb lives in the active perfect must have misheard, and ✗ I was misheard by him is barely used.

entries.meaning: Beat someone or something in sales — move more units than the competition.
examples: Their small team outsold the entire regional office last quarter.
No dealership in the state can outsell them on used trucks.
By December the franchise had outsold every other location.
Trucks outsell sedans in most of the country.
The paperback will probably outsell the hardcover ten to one.
That one album has outsold everything else the label ever released.
Nothing on the menu outsells the breakfast burrito.

senses.head: Sell more than a competitor
body: Of a company, a store, or a salesperson. The object is the rival, not the goods: outsold Ford, outsold the whole team. (продавать больше, чем (конкурент))
examples: Their small team outsold the entire regional office last quarter.
No dealership in the state can outsell them on used trucks.
By December the franchise had outsold every other location.

senses.head: Of a product: sell in greater numbers
body: Here both subject and object are goods, and the comparison is units moved. For price it is undersell; for hype it is oversell. (продаваться лучше, чем)
examples: Trucks outsell sedans in most of the country.
The paperback will probably outsell the hardcover ten to one.
That one album has outsold everything else the label ever released.
Nothing on the menu outsells the breakfast burrito.

entries.register: rare — a prefixed derivative confined to business and trade writing; in conversation an American says sold more than
entries.contrast: Three prefixed forms of sell sit close together and mean different things: outsell is about volume (you sold more than the other guy), undersell is about price (you charged less), and oversell is about promising more than you can deliver. The object of outsell may be the rival or the rival's product: outsold Ford, outsold every other pickup.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, reporting a result over a period: trucks outsell sedans in most of the country.
entries.transitivity: transitive — object obligatory, and it names the rival or the rival's product, never the goods you moved: outsold Ford, outsold every other pickup, ✗ outsold ten thousand trucks.
entries.passive: yes, though the active carries most of the traffic: sedans are outsold by trucks nearly everywhere, the hardcover was outsold ten to one.

entries.meaning: Hear what was not meant for you — by accident, not by design.
examples: In an open office you overhear everything.
I overheard two nurses talking about the schedule.
They had overheard the whole argument through the wall.
She has overheard enough to guess what the meeting was about.
The senator was overheard telling an aide the deal was dead.
He has been overheard complaining about the new policy more than once.

senses.head: Accidentally hear
body: In American usage the accident is built into the word: you were there and the words reached you. Deliberate listening is eavesdrop, which is regular — eavesdropped. (нечаянно услышать, случайно подслушать)
examples: In an open office you overhear everything.
I overheard two nurses talking about the schedule.
They had overheard the whole argument through the wall.
She has overheard enough to guess what the meeting was about.

senses.head: be overheard saying something
body: The passive is a journalistic staple: someone is caught saying in private what they would not have said publicly. (быть услышанным, попасться на словах)
examples: The senator was overheard telling an aide the deal was dead.
He has been overheard complaining about the new policy more than once.

entries.register: everyday — prefixed, but fully current: I overheard them talking is ordinary conversation
entries.contrast: Inflects like hear. In American usage overhear is accidental — you were there and the words reached you. Deliberate listening is eavesdrop (regular: eavesdropped), so the Russian gloss splits across two English verbs: I overheard them arguing is innocent, I was eavesdropping is not.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic but involuntary; deliberate listening is the separate regular verb eavesdrop. Commonly takes an -ing clause: overheard two nurses talking.
entries.transitivity: transitive — object obligatory: in an open office you overhear everything, they had overheard the whole argument. ✗ I overheard alone leaves the sentence hanging.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is a journalistic staple: the senator was overheard telling an aide the deal was dead, he has been overheard complaining more than once.

entries.meaning: Sell more of something than exists, or claim more for it than it can deliver.
examples: Airlines routinely oversell popular routes.
The venue oversold the show by two hundred seats.
Our flight had been oversold, and four of us volunteered to wait.
Try not to oversell the software in the demo.
The company has oversold this product for years.
Every ad oversells something.
Traders had oversold the sector by early spring.
The index looks oversold after five straight down days.

senses.head: Sell more than you have
body: Airlines, hotels, and venues deliberately book past capacity. Usually passive when it lands on you. Not the same as sell out, which just means the stock is gone. (продавать больше, чем есть в наличии)
examples: Airlines routinely oversell popular routes.
The venue oversold the show by two hundred seats.
Our flight had been oversold, and four of us volunteered to wait.

senses.head: Overhype, promise too much
body: Praising a product, an idea, or a person past what they can deliver. Often a warning to the speaker: don't oversell it. (перехваливать, преувеличивать достоинства)
examples: Try not to oversell the software in the demo.
The company has oversold this product for years.
Every ad oversells something.

senses.head: oversold — a market that has fallen too far
body: Finance only, and only in the participle: prices have dropped further than the fundamentals justify, so traders expect a bounce. The opposite is overbought. (перепроданный (о рынке, бумаге))
examples: Traders had oversold the sector by early spring.
The index looks oversold after five straight down days.

entries.register: neutral — airline and marketing vocabulary, but the flight was oversold and don't oversell it come out without effort
entries.contrast: Inflects like sell. Two senses in American English: selling more of a thing than actually exists (airlines oversell flights) and praising something past what it can deliver (don't oversell the feature). Selling your whole stock is a different phrase — sell out, sold out — so a concert that sold out is good news and a flight that was oversold is not.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both the capacity sense (airlines oversell popular routes) and the hype sense (don't oversell the feature). The participle oversold is also a finance adjective: the index looks oversold.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the venue oversold the show by two hundred seats, the company has oversold this product for years; the object is normally required.
entries.passive: yes, and it is the usual form when the booking lands on you: our flight had been oversold, traders had oversold the sector → the sector had been oversold by spring.

entries.meaning: Hear a case again — a courtroom term, not a word for playing something back.
examples: Appellate courts rarely rehear a case they have already decided.
The panel agreed to rehear the appeal en banc.
The circuit court reheard the matter in March.
The case has been reheard twice.
By then the judges had reheard the arguments and changed nothing.

senses.head: Hear a case again in court
body: American legal English only: an appellate court takes back a matter it has already decided, often en banc. For music or a recording say listen to it again, never ✗ rehear it — and it has nothing to do with rehearse, which is regular and belongs to the theater. (пересматривать дело, слушать повторно)
examples: Appellate courts rarely rehear a case they have already decided.
The panel agreed to rehear the appeal en banc.
The circuit court reheard the matter in March.
The case has been reheard twice.
By then the judges had reheard the arguments and changed nothing.

entries.register: rare — specialized to American appellate procedure; outside a courtroom nobody produces it
entries.third person: rehears · -ing form: rehearing — normally a noun in American legal English: the court granted a rehearing
entries.contrast: Inflects like hear, but the word is a courtroom term: a court rehears a case. For music or a recording, American English says listen to it again or play it back, never ✗ rehear it. It has nothing to do with rehearse, which is regular (rehearsed) and belongs to the theater.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and narrowly institutional: an appellate court takes a matter back up. Not a word for playing a recording again.
entries.transitivity: transitive — object obligatory and restricted to a case, an appeal, or arguments: rehear the appeal en banc, ✗ rehear the album (say listen to it again).
entries.passive: yes — the case has been reheard twice, the arguments had been reheard and nothing changed; the passive is as common as the active in opinions.

entries.meaning: Sell on what you bought instead of keeping it.
examples: Scalpers buy tickets in bulk and resell them at four times face value.
She resold the bike a month later for more than she paid.
The apartment had been resold twice before we ever saw it.
The store resells refurbished laptops with a one-year warranty.
That dealer has resold the same painting three times.
They resell enterprise software to hospitals.
I had to resell the board on a plan they had already approved.
By Friday she had resold the whole team on the deadline.

senses.head: Sell something you bought
body: The buyer turns around and becomes the seller, usually at a markup. Stress falls on the second syllable of the verb, /ˌriˈsɛl/, but on the first of the noun resale. (перепродавать)
examples: Scalpers buy tickets in bulk and resell them at four times face value.
She resold the bike a month later for more than she paid.
The apartment had been resold twice before we ever saw it.

senses.head: Distribute another company's product
body: Commercial: a reseller buys wholesale and sells on under its own contract. Very common in software, hardware, and refurbished goods. (перепродавать (как дистрибьютор))
examples: The store resells refurbished laptops with a one-year warranty.
That dealer has resold the same painting three times.
They resell enterprise software to hospitals.

senses.head: resell someone on — persuade again
body: Figurative, built on sell someone on an idea: winning back agreement that has quietly slipped away. (заново убеждать кого-л.)
examples: I had to resell the board on a plan they had already approved.
By Friday she had resold the whole team on the deadline.

entries.register: neutral — commerce and ticket talk; ordinary in writing and common enough in speech about resale
entries.contrast: Inflects like sell. The verb takes its stress on the second syllable, /ˌriˈsɛl/, while the related noun resale takes it on the first, /ˈriseɪl/: he resold the ticket, but a resale shop.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all senses, including the figurative resell the board on a plan they had already approved.
entries.transitivity: transitive — object obligatory: resell them at four times face value, resells refurbished laptops. The persuasion sense adds an on-phrase: resold the whole team on the deadline.
entries.passive: yes — the apartment had been resold twice before we ever saw it; the same painting has been resold three times.

entries.meaning: Tell a story again — usually in a new shape.
examples: Every generation retells the same handful of stories.
Let me retell it the way my grandmother did.
The story has been retold on stage, on film, and in a graphic novel.
He retold the joke badly and nobody laughed.
She had retold the accident so many times that the details had smoothed out.
The guide retells the town's founding legend at every stop.

senses.head: Tell a story again, in a new form
body: Adaptation: myths, folktales, and films get retold for a new audience. The noun a retelling is as common as the verb itself. (пересказывать, излагать заново)
examples: Every generation retells the same handful of stories.
Let me retell it the way my grandmother did.
The story has been retold on stage, on film, and in a graphic novel.

senses.head: Recount something over and over
body: Repeating your own account of an event. Note that retell takes the story as its object, never the listener: ✗ retell them the address — say tell them again. (рассказывать снова и снова)
examples: He retold the joke badly and nobody laughed.
She had retold the accident so many times that the details had smoothed out.
The guide retells the town's founding legend at every stop.

entries.register: neutral — mostly written, and mostly about stories; speech says tell it again
entries.third person: retells · -ing form: retelling (also a noun: a modern retelling of the myth)
entries.contrast: Inflects like tell. Retell means telling a story again, usually in a new shape; for repeating a fact to someone, American English says tell them again or repeat it, not ✗ retell them the address.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; the -ing form doubles as a noun, a modern retelling of the myth.
entries.transitivity: transitive, and unlike tell it is not ditransitive: the object must be the story, never the listener — retold the joke badly, ✗ retell them the address (say tell them again).
entries.passive: yes — the story has been retold on stage, on film, and in a graphic novel.

entries.meaning: Boil or churn — and, in today's English, be furious without showing it.
examples: Whenever the subject comes up, he seethes.
She seethed through the entire meeting and never said a word.
The newsroom had seethed for a week before anyone quit.
The station seethed with commuters.
The department has seethed with rumors since the merger.
By nine the sidewalk seethes with tourists.
You can watch the water seethe where the river hits the rocks.
The surf seethed over the rocks all night.
The pot had seethed down to nothing while she was on the phone.
In the King James Bible, "Jacob sod pottage" — that is, he boiled it.
The old perfect ran on the same form: by nightfall they had sod the meat.
Three days of rain left the field sodden, which is all that remains of the old participle.

senses.head: Be quietly furious
body: The dominant modern sense: anger held in rather than let out. Here the verb is regular — seethed, have seethed — and ✗ sod is impossible. (кипеть от злости, негодовать)
examples: Whenever the subject comes up, he seethes.
She seethed through the entire meeting and never said a word.
The newsroom had seethed for a week before anyone quit.

senses.head: seethe with — churn, be crowded with
body: Of a place full of moving people, or of an atmosphere thick with rumor or resentment. Regular forms only. (кишеть, бурлить (чем-л.))
examples: The station seethed with commuters.
The department has seethed with rumors since the merger.
By nine the sidewalk seethes with tourists.

senses.head: Boil, churn (of liquid)
body: The original literal sense, now literary — ordinary cooking uses boil. Modern usage is regular. (кипеть, бурлить (о жидкости))
examples: You can watch the water seethe where the river hits the rocks.
The surf seethed over the rocks all night.
The pot had seethed down to nothing while she was on the phone.

senses.head: Archaic: boil something (sod)
body: Dead in modern English, and listed only because it is where this group's forms sod / sod come from. It survives as the noun sod (a strip of turf) and the adjective sodden. (варить, кипятить (устар.))
examples: In the King James Bible, "Jacob sod pottage" — that is, he boiled it.
The old perfect ran on the same form: by nightfall they had sod the meat.
Three days of rain left the field sodden, which is all that remains of the old participle.

entries.register: neutral to formal — the anger sense is at home in writing and understood by everyone; the strong forms sod and sodden are archaic
entries.contrast: This is the one entry in the group whose old forms are no longer live. In modern American English seethe is a regular verb — seethed, have seethed — and sod survives only as a noun meaning a strip of turf. The old participle left a fossil behind as well: sodden, now purely an adjective meaning soaked through. Write the crowd seethed, never ✗ the crowd sod. The meaning has drifted too: literal boiling is now boil, and seethe usually describes anger that stays silent.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a continuing process, and comfortable in the progressive: the sidewalk was seething with tourists. Modern American forms are regular (seethed, have seethed); ✗ the crowd sod.
entries.transitivity: intransitive in every live sense — he seethes, the station seethed with commuters — and what it churns with follows with. Only the dead archaic "boil something" sense was transitive: Jacob sod pottage.
entries.passive: no — an intransitive verb has no passive: ✗ the meeting was seethed through. The archaic transitive use left behind only the adjective sodden.

entries.meaning: Hand something over in exchange for money — and, figuratively, get an idea or a person accepted.
examples: We sold the truck to a neighbor.
The house has sold twice since we moved out.
They want to sell before the school year starts.
They sell coffee beans by the pound.
He sells insurance in three states.
The corner store has sold newspapers since 1948.
Nothing is selling this month.
The album sold two million copies in a year.
Winter coats sell fast once the weather turns.
By Friday the bakery had sold out of every loaf.
Tickets sold out in eleven minutes.
The tour has sold out three nights running.
Fans said the band sold out the moment the ad aired.
He sold his partners out to avoid charges.
She felt they had sold out everything the campaign stood for.
I couldn't sell the committee on the idea.
She had sold everyone on the move within a week.
Good luck selling him on a six a.m. flight.
I am not sold on the new design.
After the demo the whole team was sold on it.
The airline sold off its regional routes.
They have sold off most of the land already.
By 2019 the family had sold off everything but the mill.
You have to sell yourself in the first two minutes.
He sold himself short in the interview and knew it.
She has sold herself well at every stage of her career.

senses.head: Exchange something for money
body: The core transitive sense, with the buyer marked by to. There is no ✗ selled: sold fills both the past and the participle, and it sounds exactly like soled. (продавать)
examples: We sold the truck to a neighbor.
The house has sold twice since we moved out.
They want to sell before the school year starts.

senses.head: Deal in, carry as stock
body: Of a business: what it offers generally, not one transaction. The subject is the shop or the person whose trade it is. (торговать чем-л., держать в продаже)
examples: They sell coffee beans by the pound.
He sells insurance in three states.
The corner store has sold newspapers since 1948.

senses.head: Of goods: be bought, move
body: Intransitive, with the merchandise as subject. Usually with an adverb (sell well, sell fast) or a figure. (продаваться, идти (о товаре))
examples: Nothing is selling this month.
The album sold two million copies in a year.
Winter coats sell fast once the weather turns.

senses.head: sell out — run out of stock
body: The stock is gone, and for a show that is good news. Do not confuse it with oversell, which is booking past capacity. (распродать; быть распроданным)
examples: By Friday the bakery had sold out of every loaf.
Tickets sold out in eleven minutes.
The tour has sold out three nights running.

senses.head: sell out — betray your principles or your side
body: Informal and disapproving. Sell someone out is betraying a particular person for your own gain. (продаться, предать)
examples: Fans said the band sold out the moment the ad aired.
He sold his partners out to avoid charges.
She felt they had sold out everything the campaign stood for.

senses.head: sell someone on — persuade
body: Getting agreement rather than money. What you are persuading them of follows on. (убедить кого-л. в чём-л.)
examples: I couldn't sell the committee on the idea.
She had sold everyone on the move within a week.
Good luck selling him on a six a.m. flight.

senses.head: be sold on — be convinced
body: The passive of the previous sense, and mostly used in the negative: I'm not sold on it yet. (быть убеждённым в чём-л.)
examples: I am not sold on the new design.
After the demo the whole team was sold on it.

senses.head: sell off — dispose of assets
body: Business usage: getting rid of a division, a holding, or excess inventory, usually cheaply or under pressure. The noun is a selloff. (распродавать (активы))
examples: The airline sold off its regional routes.
They have sold off most of the land already.
By 2019 the family had sold off everything but the mill.

senses.head: sell yourself — present yourself well
body: In interviews and pitches. The matching failure is sell yourself short — undervaluing what you can do. (подать себя, показать себя с лучшей стороны)
examples: You have to sell yourself in the first two minutes.
He sold himself short in the interview and knew it.
She has sold herself well at every stage of her career.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: There is no ✗ selled, and sold covers both slots: we sold it in June, we have sold three. Sold is pronounced exactly like soled, as in resoled shoes. The noun is sale, not sell: the sale of the house, ✗ the sell of the house. And sell out / sold out means the stock is gone, which is not what oversell means.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout, including the figurative sell someone on an idea and sell yourself in an interview.
entries.transitivity: both — ditransitive or transitive with to (sold a neighbor the truck / sold the truck to a neighbor), and intransitive with the merchandise as subject, usually with an adverb or a figure (winter coats sell fast, the album sold two million copies).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the house has been sold twice since we moved out, I am not sold on the new design. The goods-as-subject use has no matching passive: winter coats sell fast is not ✗ winter coats are sold fast.
entries.phrasal verbs: sell off · sell on · sell out · sell out of · sell short · sell up

entries.meaning: Put shoes on — most often on a horse.
examples: A good farrier can shoe a horse in half an hour.
They shod the whole string before the trail ride.
Every horse in the barn has been shod this season.
The stable shoes about thirty animals a month.
The mission fed and shod everyone who came through the door.
By winter the charity had shod four hundred kids.
The children arrived shod in boots two sizes too big.
A well-shod horse rarely goes lame.
The mare had been shod badly and had gone lame.
Management rode roughshod over the union's objections.
The new rule has ridden roughshod over forty years of practice.

senses.head: Fit a horse with horseshoes
body: The live sense of the verb, and the one where shod is nearly the only past you will meet. The person who does it is a farrier. (подковывать)
examples: A good farrier can shoe a horse in half an hour.
They shod the whole string before the trail ride.
Every horse in the barn has been shod this season.
The stable shoes about thirty animals a month.

senses.head: Put shoes on a person
body: Formal or literary; everyday American says put shoes on a child rather than shoe him. The regular shoed is acceptable here, though shod is standard. (обувать)
examples: The mission fed and shod everyone who came through the door.
By winter the charity had shod four hundred kids.
The children arrived shod in boots two sizes too big.

senses.head: shod as an adjective — fitted, sheathed
body: The participle does most of its modern work as an adjective, with a modifier attached: well-shod, poorly shod, rubber-shod, steel-shod. (обутый; подкованный; окованный)
examples: A well-shod horse rarely goes lame.
The mare had been shod badly and had gone lame.

senses.head: ride roughshod over — trample, ignore
body: A frozen idiom built on the old participle: overriding someone's rights, objections, or feelings entirely. Roughshod survives nowhere else in the language. (не считаться с кем-л., попирать)
examples: Management rode roughshod over the union's objections.
The new rule has ridden roughshod over forty years of practice.

entries.register: rare — a farrier's word for horses; shod survives mostly as an adjective in well-shod and roughshod
entries.third person: shoes /ʃuz/ · -ing form: shoeing (the e stays — ✗ shoing)
entries.contrast: The regular shoed is also acceptable, but shod is the standard American form, and with horses it is nearly the only one you will see: the farrier shod four horses. The participle now does most of its work as an adjective — well-shod, poorly shod, and the frozen roughshod in ride roughshod over someone. For people, everyday American prefers a phrase: you put shoes on a toddler rather than shoe him.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; the participle shod now does most of its work as an adjective (well-shod, steel-shod) and survives frozen in ride roughshod over.
entries.transitivity: transitive — object obligatory: shoe a horse in half an hour, fed and shod everyone who came through the door. ✗ The farrier shod alone is incomplete.
entries.passive: yes, and it is the common form — every horse in the barn has been shod this season, the mare had been shod badly and had gone lame.

entries.meaning: Give someone information — say something to a listener, narrate it, instruct them, or make it out.
examples: She told me the flight had been canceled.
Don't tell him about the party.
We have told the landlord three times.
He tells the story better than anyone.
I tell my students the same thing every fall.
By then he had told the story to everyone in the building.
The officer told us to stay in the car.
I have told her twice not to leave the gate open.
Tell him to call me when he lands.
I can't tell the twins apart.
You could tell from her face that the news was bad.
There is no telling how long the repair will take.
He told the truth and got fired for it.
She is six and can already tell time.
To tell you the truth, I had never told anyone that story before.
Twelve-hour shifts began to tell on him.
The years have told on that engine.
If you break it, I am telling on you.
His brother told on him.
Someone had told on them before the shift ended.
She told him off in front of the whole team.
I have never been told off like that in my life.
He couldn't resist saying I told you so.
You never can tell with that crowd.

senses.head: Give someone information
body: Tell needs a listener and takes one bare (tell me), while say refuses a bare listener: ✗ He told that he was late, ✗ He said me he was late. (говорить, сообщать кому-л.)
examples: She told me the flight had been canceled.
Don't tell him about the party.
We have told the landlord three times.

senses.head: Narrate, relate
body: Of a story, a joke, or an account, with or without a listener named. (рассказывать)
examples: He tells the story better than anyone.
I tell my students the same thing every fall.
By then he had told the story to everyone in the building.

senses.head: tell someone to — instruct, order
body: With an infinitive this is a plain order or instruction; the negative is tell someone not to, with not before the infinitive. (велеть, приказывать)
examples: The officer told us to stay in the car.
I have told her twice not to leave the gate open.
Tell him to call me when he lands.

senses.head: Make out, distinguish
body: Almost always with can, could, or be able to: perceiving a difference or working something out from evidence. Hence tell the difference, tell them apart, tell by. (определять, различать)
examples: I can't tell the twins apart.
You could tell from her face that the news was bad.
There is no telling how long the repair will take.

senses.head: tell the truth, tell a lie, tell time
body: A short fixed list where only tell works: ✗ say the truth, ✗ read the time. To tell you the truth also opens a sentence as a discourse marker. (говорить правду; лгать; определять время по часам)
examples: He told the truth and got fired for it.
She is six and can already tell time.
To tell you the truth, I had never told anyone that story before.

senses.head: tell on — show the strain
body: Intransitive, of stress, age, or long hours gradually having a visible effect on a person or a machine. (сказываться на ком-л.)
examples: Twelve-hour shifts began to tell on him.
The years have told on that engine.

senses.head: tell on someone — inform, snitch
body: Children's usage first, but it carries into adult talk about reporting someone to an authority. (ябедничать, доносить на кого-л.)
examples: If you break it, I am telling on you.
His brother told on him.
Someone had told on them before the shift ended.

senses.head: tell someone off — scold
body: Informal and separable: a sharp reprimand delivered face to face. (отчитать, отругать)
examples: She told him off in front of the whole team.
I have never been told off like that in my life.

senses.head: I told you so, you never can tell
body: Two fixed formulas: the first claims vindication after the fact, the second admits that nothing here can be predicted. (я же говорил; никогда не знаешь)
examples: He couldn't resist saying I told you so.
You never can tell with that crowd.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.third person: tells · -ing form: telling (also an adjective: a telling detail)
entries.contrast: No ✗ telled, and no past/participle swap to worry about, since told is both. The real trap is tell against say: tell needs a listener and takes one bare (tell me, told her the truth), while say refuses a bare listener (said to me). ✗ He told that he was late, ✗ He said me he was late. Tell is also the verb in a short fixed list: tell the truth, tell a lie, tell time, tell the difference, tell them apart.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the reporting, narrating, and instructing senses; closer to stative in can tell "perceive, work out," which leans on a modal and rejects the progressive: ✗ I am telling the twins apart.
entries.transitivity: ditransitive at its core, with the listener bare and obligatory — told me the flight had been canceled, ✗ told to me, ✗ He told that he was late. Also plain transitive in the fixed list (tell the truth, tell time) and intransitive with on (the years have told on that engine).
entries.passive: yes — we were told to stay in the car, I have never been told off like that in my life. The listener is the natural passive subject: she was told the news, while the news was told to her is stiff.
entries.phrasal verbs: tell apart · tell off · tell on

entries.meaning: Charge less than the competition — or describe something as less than it is.
examples: Nobody in the county can undersell them on lumber.
The chain undersold every local shop and then raised its prices.
Warehouse clubs undersell supermarkets on nearly everything.
The brochure badly undersells the view.
Reviewers have undersold how strange the film is.
He had undersold his own experience in the interview and knew it.
Don't undersell yourself — that work took months.
Their bid has undersold the team's expertise by a wide margin.

senses.head: Charge less than a competitor
body: The comparison is price, not volume. Compare outsell, which is more units, and oversell, which is more promise than product. (продавать дешевле конкурентов)
examples: Nobody in the county can undersell them on lumber.
The chain undersold every local shop and then raised its prices.
Warehouse clubs undersell supermarkets on nearly everything.

senses.head: Understate, describe too modestly
body: Of a description that fails to do justice to the thing — a brochure, a title, a summary, a review. (преуменьшать, недооценивать (достоинства))
examples: The brochure badly undersells the view.
Reviewers have undersold how strange the film is.

senses.head: undersell yourself — undervalue what you offer
body: Reflexive: asking too little for your work, or presenting your own experience as smaller than it is. (недооценивать себя, продешевить)
examples: He had undersold his own experience in the interview and knew it.
Don't undersell yourself — that work took months.
Their bid has undersold the team's expertise by a wide margin.

entries.register: rare — a prefixed derivative kept alive by trade writing; ordinary speech says cheaper than
entries.contrast: Inflects like sell. Two senses, both of them "less": charging less than a rival (they undersell every store in town) and describing something more modestly than it deserves (the brochure undersells the view). Compare outsell, which is more units, and oversell, which is more promise than product.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, comparing price (the chain undersold every local shop) or the fit between a description and its subject (the brochure badly undersells the view).
entries.transitivity: transitive — object obligatory, naming the rival or the thing described, not the price: undersell them on lumber, undersells the view, reflexive in don't undersell yourself.
entries.passive: yes — every local shop was undersold by the chain. The "understate" sense passivizes less comfortably and is usually left in the active: reviewers have undersold how strange the film is.
